prime.problem: A neural net takes a fixed number of inputs and needs a target to compare against. A file of names of different lengths is neither, so without a conversion step there is nothing to train on.
prime.fits: The bigram lecture turned names into (char → next char) pairs. This card widens the left side to three characters, which is the input the Bengio-style MLP in the rest of this course expects.
prime.goal: Write build_dataset, predict how many rows any list of names gives, and explain why the padding is what lets the model start and end names.

attend: Why does the context start as [0, 0, 0] rather than as the first three letters of the name?
Which single line makes the window slide, and why does it build a new list instead of changing the old one?
Why does the number of rows stay at 228,146 whatever block_size you choose?
What does the loop add at the end of every name, and what would the model never learn without it?
Why do five different labels end up sharing the context ..., and what does that cost later?

must: Every name starts from the all-dots context → the first letter becomes the label of a ... row → the model learns how names start, and sampling can begin from ...
One row per character read (letters plus the end dot) → rows = Σ(len(w) + 1) → 32 rows for 5 names, 228,146 for all, independent of block_size → a longer context widens X, it doesn't lengthen it
context[1:] + [ix] drops the oldest id and appends the newest → every row has exactly block_size inputs → a fixed-width X that a weight matrix can multiply
The same context can come with different labels (... → e, o, a, i, s) → no model can fit every row → even a perfect fit to these 32 rows keeps a loss above 0
elevated: context[1:] + [ix] creates a new list → the list already appended to X is never changed → an in-place context.pop(0); context.append(ix) would make every row of X point at the same final list
reference: the lab prints rows as ctx ---> ch
names.txt: 32,033 names, 2 to 15 letters, 196,113 letters in total

compress.prompt: Without scrolling up, explain in 3–5 sentences how a list of names becomes X and Y. Or draw the window for ava and write each row with its integers.
checklist: for each char in w + '.': save (context, char) as one row, then crop the oldest and append the new char
rows per name = letters + 1, so 5 names → 32 rows and all names → 228,146
X is (N, block_size) integer ids; Y is (N,) ids of the next char
the padding lets the model learn starts (... rows) and ends (label .)

retrieve.q: Explain why the dataset pads the start of each name with dots but only adds a single dot at the end.
answer: the start padding fills the context so the first letter can be a label with a full-width input
the end needs only one dot because the dot is a label there, the char meaning "stop"
together they let the model learn both how names begin and when they end

retrieve.q: Walk ava through build_dataset with block_size 3: list every row as context → label, with the integer ids.
answer: 4 rows = 3 letters + 1

retrieve.q: You raise block_size from 3 to 8. What happens to the number of rows, the shape of X, and how much of each short name's rows is padding? What do you gain and what does it cost?
answer: rows stay 228,146; X becomes (228146, 8)
short names become mostly dots: emma's last row is ....emma
gain: the model can see further back
cost: more inputs per row, so a bigger first layer, and more parameters to train

retrieve.q: Your 5-name dataset has 32 rows. Someone drops the start padding and keeps only real 3-letter windows. How many rows survive, and which predictions can the model no longer learn?
answer: 17 rows survive (15 fewer)
the first three letters of every name are never labels
so the model can't learn how names start, and sampling has no starting context

compare.q: The bigram lecture's pairs vs this card's rows: what is the same, what changed, and why did the change force a switch from counting to a neural net?
answer: same: one example per character to predict, 228,146 in all, with . for start and end
changed: the input is 3 characters, not 1
a count table would need 27³ = 19,683 rows, most of them unseen
a net with shared embeddings can generalise to contexts it rarely or never saw

compare.q: This card builds every window up front into X. The GPT lecture instead keeps the text as one tensor and cuts random chunks at training time. What does each design cost, and when would you pick each?
answer: up front: simple and easy to inspect, but it stores each char up to block_size times
on the fly: stores the text once, and every position inside a chunk is a target
up front is fine for 228,146 rows × 3; on the fly is necessary for long contexts and large corpora

predict.q: Change block_size to 8 and rebuild the dataset from all names. Before running it: what is X.shape, and what is emma's last row?
predict.answer: X.shape is (228146, 8): the row count doesn't change, because it only depends on how many characters are read. Emma's last row is ....emma → ., half padding. With a context this long, most names are mostly dots in their early rows.

apply.task: Invert the dataset: using only X and Y from build_dataset(words[:5]) (not words), rebuild the five names. Use itos to turn ids back into characters.
apply.done: Your function prints emma, olivia, ava, isabella, sophia, and finds that the names start at rows 0, 5, 12, 16 and 25.
apply.hint: A new name starts wherever the row of X is all zeros. Collect Y from there until you hit a label of 0.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 32 rows, or the count staying at 228,146 when block_size changes?
What couldn't you explain cleanly: why the start gets three dots but the end only one?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: padding → rows that start names, or shared ... context → a loss that can't reach 0?
Could you write build_dataset again from a blank file, without looking?
What will you check first when a later card's X.shape doesn't match what you expect?
